title: Series and parallel circuits — how components are connected matters
examTip: Expect 'state the rule', calculation and 'explain why' questions. One favourite keeps coming back: why household circuits are wired in parallel.
introTips: This covers the rules for current, potential difference and resistance in series and parallel circuits
You will work through calculations for series circuits, and learn the rules for parallel circuits
By the end, you will be able to set up and read circuit diagrams. You will also be able to explain why real circuits are wired the way they are
intro: Components can be joined in a single loop or in separate branches. That choice completely changes how a circuit behaves. Get it wrong in a circuit diagram and everything after it is wrong. Series and parallel rules come up in calculations and in 'explain' questions. They also explain everyday things. For example, one blown bulb used to knock out a whole string of Christmas lights. Knowing both types gives you the tools to work out any circuit you are given.

basics.text: A circuit is a complete loop of wire that charge can flow round. It is like a running track: you end up back where you started. If there is a gap anywhere, nothing flows.
Current is how much electric charge flows past a point each second. Think of cars passing under a bridge: more cars each second is a bigger flow. It is measured in amperes (A), often called amps.
Potential difference is the push that makes charge move round a circuit. A cell or battery gives it. It is measured in volts (V), and a bigger number means a bigger push.

Resistance is how hard it is for current to get through something. It is like a narrow, crowded corridor that slows people down. More resistance means less current for the same push. It is measured in ohms (Ω).
A branch is where a wire splits into two paths that join up again. It is like a road that splits round an island and meets again. Charge can go either way.

keyPoints.heading: Series circuits — one loop, shared everything
keyPoints.content: In a series circuit, components are joined in a single continuous loop with no branches. So there is only one path for charge to flow. This leads to three key rules. First, current is the same everywhere in the circuit. If 2 A flows through one component, 2 A flows through all of them. Second, the total potential difference of the supply is shared between the components. Say a battery gives 12 V and one resistor has 8 V across it. Then the other has 4 V. Third, the total resistance is the sum of all individual resistances: Rtotal = R1 + R2 + R3 + ... For example, two resistors of 3 Ω and 5 Ω in series give a total resistance of 3 + 5 = 8 Ω. Adding more resistors to a series circuit always increases the total resistance. This is because the same current has to pass through each resistor in turn. Each one adds its own opposition. So the current from the supply falls. To find the current, use current = potential difference ÷ total resistance (I = V ÷ Rtotal).
writeBullets: Series circuit — a single loop with no branches. Only one path for current
Current — the same at every point in a series circuit
Potential difference — the total p.d. of the supply is shared between the components
Total resistance — Rtotal = R1 + R2 + R3 (resistances add up in series)
Current from the supply — I = V ÷ Rtotal
Adding resistors — increases the total resistance, so the current from the supply falls
Consequence — if one component breaks in series, the circuit is broken and all components stop

keyTerms.def: Components connected in a single loop with no branches; current has only one path
Sum of individual resistances: Rtotal = R1 + R2 + ...

keyPoints.memTip: Series = Same current. 'S for Same, S for Series.' Potential difference is shared, and resistances add.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Examiners love giving you the supply potential difference and the p.d. across one component. Then they ask for the p.d. across the other. Remember: the p.d.s must add up to the supply.

keyPoints.heading: Parallel circuits — branches give choice
keyPoints.content: In a parallel circuit, components are joined in separate branches between the same two points. Charge can take different routes. This leads to three rules that are very different from series. First, the potential difference across each component in parallel is the same. This is because each branch connects the same two points. Second, the current splits between branches. The branch with lower resistance carries more current. The total current from the supply equals the sum of the branch currents. Third, the total resistance is less than the smallest individual resistance. Adding branches gives charge more routes, so it flows more easily overall. So the total resistance of two resistors in parallel is less than the resistance of the smaller one. Some circuits include both series and parallel parts.
writeBullets: Parallel circuit — components in separate branches. Many paths for current
Potential difference — the same across each component in parallel
Current — splits between branches. More current goes through the branch with lower resistance
Total current — sum of all branch currents
Total resistance — less than the smallest individual resistance

keyTerms.def: Components in separate branches between the same two points; the potential difference across each component is the same
Always less than the resistance of the smallest individual resistor

keyPoints.memTip: Parallel = same potential difference. Current splits like traffic at a junction. Total resistance is less than the smallest resistor.
keyPoints.tutor_note: A common mistake is thinking parallel resistance is an average. Adding a branch gives charge another route. So the total resistance goes down.

keyPoints.heading: Real-world circuits — why the wiring matters
keyPoints.content: Series and parallel help explain everyday electrical systems. Old-style Christmas tree lights were wired in series. When one bulb blew, the circuit broke and the whole string went out. Lights wired in parallel keep working if one bulb fails. Each bulb has its own branch. Household mains wiring is always parallel. Each socket and appliance is on a separate branch, connected directly to the 230 V supply. This gives three benefits: - every device gets the full supply potential difference (needed for devices designed for 230 V) - each can be switched on and off on its own - a fault in one appliance doesn't cut power to everything else If household circuits were in series, switching off your phone charger would turn off everything else too. That would clearly not work.
writeBullets: Christmas lights (series) — one bulb blows → the circuit breaks → they all go out
Lights in parallel — one bulb fails → the other branches keep working
Household circuits — always parallel. Each device is on its own branch
Full potential difference — with parallel wiring, every appliance gets the full 230 V supply
Separate switching — each branch can be controlled on its own
Fault isolation — a fault in one appliance doesn't cut power to the whole circuit

keyTerms.def: Mains circuits wired so every appliance gets full supply potential difference and can be switched independently

keyPoints.memTip: House = Parallel. Phone charger off, lights still on. That is parallel in action.
keyPoints.tutor_note: In 'explain why' questions about household wiring, you need TWO separate points. Give full potential difference to each device AND separate switching. One alone is unlikely to earn full marks.

keyPoints.heading: Calculating values in series circuits
keyPoints.content: Many questions ask you to find the current or potential difference in a series circuit. Use the idea of equivalent resistance. This is one resistance that has the same effect as the whole combination. Step 1: Add the series resistors to find the total resistance: Rtotal = R1 + R2. Step 2: Use the supply potential difference to find the current: I = V ÷ Rtotal. Step 3: Use V = IR for each resistor to find the potential difference across it. Step 4: Check that these add up to the supply potential difference. Worked example: R1 = 4 Ω and R2 = 2 Ω are in series. Supply = 12 V. Step 1: Rtotal = 4 + 2 = 6 Ω. Step 2: I = 12 ÷ 6 = 2 A. Step 3: V across R1 = 2 A × 4 Ω = 8 V. V across R2 = 2 A × 2 Ω = 4 V. Step 4: 8 + 4 = 12 V.
writeBullets: Step 1 — add the series resistors to get the total (equivalent) resistance
Step 2 — use I = V ÷ Rtotal to find the current from the supply
Step 3 — use V = IR for each resistor to find the p.d. across it
Step 4 — check the p.d.s add up to the supply potential difference

keyTerms.def: A single resistance value that has the same effect on the circuit as a combination of resistors

keyPoints.memTip: Series problems: add the resistors, then I = V ÷ R, then V = IR for each one. Then check they add up.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Always check your answer at the end. The p.d.s across each series section should add up to the supply potential difference. This takes 10 seconds. It catches arithmetic slips before they cost you marks.

keyPoints.heading: Measuring circuits — ammeters and voltmeters
keyPoints.content: To measure current, use an ammeter connected in series with the component. Then all the current you want to measure flows through the meter. To measure potential difference, use a voltmeter connected in parallel across the component. This puts it between the same two points as the component, so it measures the same p.d. A dc series circuit is useful for measuring and testing. For example, put a variable resistor in series with a component. Changing its resistance changes the current through the component. The ammeter and voltmeter then measure I and V for each setting. Common circuit diagram mistakes: - drawing the ammeter in parallel - drawing the voltmeter in series - putting meters in the wrong branch of a parallel circuit
writeBullets: Ammeter — in series with the component. Measures the current through it
Voltmeter — in parallel with the component. Measures the p.d. across it
Wrong ammeter position — in parallel. It must be in series to measure the current through the component
Wrong voltmeter position — in series. It must be in parallel to measure the p.d. across the component
Testing circuit — a variable resistor in series changes the current through the component
keyPoints.memTip: A for Ammeter = A for Along (in series, along the wire). V for Voltmeter = V shape (in parallel, spanning across).

tables.title: Series vs parallel circuits — key comparison
rows: Same at every point in the circuit
Splits between branches; total = sum of branch currents
Shared — the supply p.d. is shared between the components
Same across each component in parallel
Sum of all resistances: Rtotal = R1 + R2 + ...
Total resistance decreases; current from supply increases
Circuit breaks — all components stop working
Other branches continue to work independently
Household mains wiring, lights wired in parallel

0.question: Two resistors of 6 Ω and 10 Ω are connected in series with a 16 V supply. What is the current in the circuit?
0.correctFeedback: Correct. Rtotal = 6 + 10 = 16 Ω; I = V/R = 16/16 = 1 A. A textbook series circuit calculation.
0.wrongFeedback: Step 1: add the resistances. Rtotal = 6 + 10 = 16 Ω. Step 2: use I = V/R = 16 ÷ 16 = 1 A. Remember, in series you always add the resistances before using I = V/R.

1.question: Resistors of 4 Ω and 12 Ω are connected in parallel. Which statement about their total resistance is correct?
options: It is between 4 Ω and 12 Ω
1.correctFeedback: Correct. In parallel, the total resistance is always less than the smallest individual resistance. Here that is less than 4 Ω.
1.wrongFeedback: Adding a parallel branch gives charge another route. So the total resistance is less than the smallest resistor, which is 4 Ω.

2.question: Why are household circuits wired in parallel?
options: Each appliance gets the full supply potential difference and can be switched on and off separately
Parallel wiring makes the current the same in every appliance
Parallel wiring increases the total resistance of the house
Parallel wiring means one switch turns everything off
2.correctFeedback: Correct. Each appliance has its own branch. So it gets the full supply potential difference and can be switched on its own.
2.wrongFeedback: In parallel, each appliance is on its own branch. It gets the full supply potential difference, and you can switch it on or off without affecting the others.

3.question: Resistors of 5 Ω and 7 Ω are in series with a 6 V supply. What is the potential difference across the 5 Ω resistor?
3.wrongFeedback: Step 1: Rtotal = 5 + 7 = 12 Ω. Step 2: I = V ÷ Rtotal = 6 ÷ 12 = 0.5 A. Step 3: V = IR = 0.5 × 5 = 2.5 V. 3.5 V is the p.d. across the 7 Ω resistor.

4.question: You want to vary the current through a lamp you are testing, in steps. What should you connect in series with it?
4.correctFeedback: Correct. Changing the resistance of a variable resistor in series changes the current through the lamp.
4.wrongFeedback: A variable resistor in series lets you change the current. A voltmeter goes in parallel, and only measures.

commonMistakes: Using series rules for parallel circuits. In parallel, the potential difference across each component is the same. It is not shared.
Thinking total parallel resistance is the average of the single resistances. It is always less than the smallest one.
Putting the ammeter in parallel instead of in series. It must be in series to measure the current through the component.
Not checking that series potential differences add up to the supply potential difference. This quick check catches arithmetic slips that would lose calculation marks.
examTips: For any series circuit calculation, always find Rtotal first by adding all the resistances. Then use I = V/Rtotal to get the current. Remember, the current is the same everywhere.
When explaining why household circuits are parallel, give two points. (1) Each device gets the full supply potential difference. (2) Devices can be switched on and off separately.
In series circuit questions, label your working clearly. For example: 'total = X + Y = Z Ω'. This makes it easy for the examiner to give partial credit.
Always check that your final answer makes physical sense. Parallel resistance must be less than the smallest branch resistance. Adding a series resistor must increase the total resistance.
revisionCardBullets: Series: current the same everywhere. The supply p.d. is shared between components. Rtotal = R1 + R2
Parallel: the p.d. across each component is the same. Current splits. Total resistance is less than the smallest resistor
Parallel total resistance is always less than the smallest individual resistance
Series — one component breaks: the whole circuit fails
Parallel — one branch breaks: the other branches keep working
Household wiring is parallel: full potential difference to each device, and separate switching
Series problems: add the resistors to find the equivalent resistance
Use I = V/R after finding Rtotal to get total current from supply
Check series answers: the p.d.s across all sections must add up to the supply potential difference
Testing circuits: a variable resistor in series changes the current through a component
